svg.text: 00 · Read this first — what it is, and how to read the page
Plain English in the big text. Real code underneath. If you read only the bold lines, you still get all of it.
The back office for a design studio. It keeps clients, projects, tasks, approvals and
deadline timers in one place, shared by the whole team.
One program: 94 endpoints, 81 live tables, 17 migration files, 13 screens. No
queue, no cache, no second service.
Every claim names the file it came from. When a box says "enforced", a line of
code enforces it and a test proves it.
The plain-English claim. Read only these and the tour still makes sense.
What RelayOS is · How it runs · The rules
The same fact with the detail that makes it useful: what, where, why it is that
"…because a build cannot see a missing setting."
The file, the line number, or the actual statement. This is the part you can check.
Depth is not in the length of the sentences. It is in every sentence being tied to a file you can open. Nothing on this page is a guess.
01 · The whole system on one napkin
Four boxes. Everything else on this page is a detail inside one of them.
Uses one browser tab. No install, no
Loads the screens once, then talks to
It serves the screens AND answers /api. One deploy, one address, one log
One database. 81 live tables. All the rules that
No queue, no worker, no cache, no object store, no second service. Each is a thing that can break, and none is needed yet.
Deliberately unauthenticated. Frame 10 says what that costs.

Why one program: the screens and the API are built and deployed together, so the browser calls /api on the address it was already loaded from. There is no second hostname, no CORS rule and no environment variable to get out of step.
02 · What you can do — and the exact endpoint behind it
Six areas of real work. The last column is the route and the line of code that serves it.
What is late, what is due this week, what is waiting on a client.
Every client, their contracts, and how far along the relationship is.
Phases, boards, budgets, and the tasks inside each column.
Create, assign, estimate, attach a checklist, record approvals step by step.
A gate that must pass before anything ships.
Timers that go running → met, missed, paused or waived.
All 94 handlers live in that one file. It is 3,370 lines long, which is the single largest piece of debt in the repository — frame 13. It is also why every route is easy to find: one file, in order.
03 · What happens when somebody clicks Save
Eleven steps, about forty milliseconds. Every step names the line that does the work.
The button sends the form to the server.
The platform sends every request to the one service.
The server matches the method and the path.
A hook runs first, on every single request.
One operator row is read and cached.
Zod parses the body. Bad input stops here.
A service performs the multi-step write.
the only place that writes tasks
The column is looked up, never guessed.
SELECT id FROM columns WHERE board_id=? AND key=?
Next key = highest suffix + 1, not row count.
One row, plus its checklist and gates.
Log, metric, and a change for other tabs.
If step 6 fails you get 400 and the field name. If step 8 fails you get 400 "unknown column". Nothing is half-written: the database refuses the whole statement, not the application.
04 · The one file to learn first — app.ts, line by line
636 lines. These thirteen are the entire request path, in the order they run.
Builds the server object. Every entrypoint calls this and nothing else.
Security headers: the page cannot be framed, sniffed or hot-linked by accident.
Allows the API to answer other origins — needed for /api in dev, harmless in prod.
A request larger than this is rejected before it reaches a handler.
First hook. Stamps the start time and resolves identity.
Counts the request, its status and its duration (RED metrics).
Any successful write appends one row, which is what the live feed reads.
One place turns any thrown error into the standard envelope.
Unknown /api path returns JSON 404, never an HTML page.
1200 / 30 / 240 requests per minute, per IP, per route class.
Attaches req.identity — the single user this deployment attributes work to.
The /api/auth/* endpoints in their own small module.
Serves a real apps/web/dist if one exists (dev). Lazily imported.

Order is the point. The error handler is registered after the hooks so it catches their failures. Static files are imported lazily — a top-level import there is exactly what caused the outage in frame 09.
05 · The database — and why bad data cannot get in
The interesting part of a table is not its columns. It is what it refuses to store.
The table that is actually created
Read the constraints as sentences: they are rules the application cannot bypass.
Ids and timestamps are decided in code
Every id is prefixed and time-sortable, so a row tells you what it is and roughly when it happened.
Timestamps are stored as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS" UTC — deliberately not ISO with a T, because a
space sorts before a T and mixing the two silently reorders every comparison.
A status outside the seven allowed values is refused by the database, whatever the client sends.
One board cannot have two columns with the same key. The database decides, not a race in the API.
Two opposite delete rules, on purpose
Deleting a project takes its tasks with it (CASCADE). Deleting a client who still has projects is refused (RESTRICT).
cl_ pr_ tsk_ usr_ — an id is self-describing, and nothing leaks how many rows exist.
Two schema sources — one of them inert
db/postgres/schema.sql calls itself "the production system of record" and carries rules the boot migrations do not, including CHECK (length(title) >= 4).
Nothing applies it automatically: migrations come from db/migrations/pg at boot, and CI never runs schema.sql. The same title rule is enforced in code
instead — zod .min(4) and a 4-character guard in the service.

81 tables are alive today, created by 83 CREATE TABLE statements — the two extra are rebuild-and-rename artefacts from the SQLite era (sessions_new, sla_timers_new), not leftovers. And the drift above is real: the code is the arbiter, so the rule that matters is
the one in routes/index.ts:392 and services/tasks.ts:99.
06 · The rules — what is enforced, and what is only a list
This is the distinction most architecture diagrams get wrong. It is the difference between a corridor and a signpost.
Enforced — the server refuses the move
A transition that is not in the table is refused with 409. Evidence rows are required for guarded moves.
dev_complete → qa_approved → lead_approved → client_accepted. Unique per task and step.
A task cannot be called done while a gate rule is unsatisfied.
A release cannot ship while a required QA check is open.
Running and past due becomes missed. Runs daily and on boot.
Only a list — nothing stops the jump
A deal can be PATCHed to any stage id. There is no server-side rule about which may follow which.
todo · doing · done is a column value, not a state machine.
columns.wip_limit is stored and seeded. Nothing reads it, so no column ever refuses a card because it is full.
Because a diagram showing a pipeline with arrows looks enforced, and a reader will believe it. It is a list of labels. Only the
left column is code that can refuse you.
An earlier version of my own board got
Plain version: a pipeline is a set of labels you can jump between. A lifecycle is a corridor with doors that only open forwards. Only the corridor is real.
07 · Two real journeys, down to the statement
One read, one write. Everything else in the API is a variation on these two.
One request, one query. The counts are correlated subqueries, so there is no N+1.
FROM projects p JOIN clients c ON …
Six steps, each one able to stop the write with a named reason.
WHERE board_id=? AND key=? → 400 no column
What the client can rely on
Every answer — success or failure — has the same outer shape. The frontend has one parser, not forty.
Two things that are easy to get wrong
A task key comes from the highest existing number, not from COUNT(*) — the count version shipped a duplicate key and a
409 in production. And the column is looked up by (board_id, key), never by guessing an id shape.
This is the level of detail the rest of the system keeps: a route, a query, a reason for the shape, and the bug that made it that way.
Four build steps, five runtime steps. Nothing compiles while a page is loading.
Build time — happens once, on Vercel, per deploy
Dev dependencies included — the build needs vite and
Vite compiles React into static files.
Those files become one TypeScript module.
Runtime — happens on every cold start
Ten reusable connections, not one per
17 SQL files, applied in order, checksummed.
Ensure exactly one users row exists.

Why step 3 of the build exists: Vercel bundles what is imported, not what sits in a folder — and the services schema rejects includeFiles. So the SPA is compiled into the API as a module (16 assets) instead of copied next to it.
09 · When it breaks — two things that really happened
Not hypotheticals. Both are in the repository, with the fix and the test that stops them returning.
Story 1 · The database that was not there
An earlier revision fell back to a file database when DATABASE_URL was missing. On a serverless host that file lives in /tmp
and is deleted with the instance — so the app booted, accepted writes, read them back, and then lost them. It behaved like a
database right up until the moment it did not. The fix was to refuse to start, and to say which setting is missing.
db/index.ts throws when neither engine is
Story 2 · The outage with no route to report it
@fastify/static was imported at the top of app.ts. Version 10.1.4 pulled in an ESM-only dependency; on a runtime without
require(esm) that threw while the module was loading — before any route existed. Every request answered boot_failed, and
nothing could explain why. The fix: pin 10.1.3, import inside the branch that needs it, and test it in a child process.
What a failure looks like now
One handler shapes every error, so a broken deployment is legible instead of blank.
Browser → a setup page naming the variable
Anything else → the same JSON envelope
Every failure that actually happened became three things: a comment in the file explaining why, a test that reproduces it,
and a line in the documentation. That is why the repository has an opinion about /tmp and about top-level imports.
Every guard in npm run verify was written
This is the part worth copying: the system is honest about how it fails, not just about what it does.
There is no login. That is a decision, and the API says so in its own response.
What the server says about itself
A reader does not have to guess whether authentication is broken — the answer
Platform password protection on the deployment, plus these application controls.
Anyone who can reach the URL can read and change everything, and every
change is filed under the same person.
RBAC exists in the schema and is never enforced
project_members, partner_iam_users and client_portal_users all exist, and scope.ts can restrict a query by membership. With a single admin operator the scope resolves
to "everything", so the restriction never fires. Saying it enforces access control would be false; saying it is absent would also be false. It is present and idle.
What turning it on would take
Four things, none of them started: an identity provider, credentials stored per user,
membership checks switched on in scope.ts, and a 403 path with tests behind it.
The honest sentence: this is an internal tool behind a platform login, not a multi-tenant product. Making it multi-tenant is a schema change plus a real identity provider — neither is done.
11 · Tests and CI — what "green" actually means
A build proves it compiles. It does not prove it starts. Both are checked, separately.
npm run verify — ten gates, in order
One command a person can run before pushing. It stops at the first failure.
guard no JSON store, SQL portable, deps declared,
migrations in sync, deployment config agrees
test:pg 19 of them again on real PostgreSQL 16
build:service the production build, exactly as Vercel runs it
verify:routing every API call in the frontend has a route
smoke:web Chromium drives the real app
verify:boot start the built server, call it, stop it
test:persistence restart and read the data back
backup:verify restore a dump into a fresh database
A build can pass while the server never starts: a missing setting, a bad top-level import, a port that is not bound. So the
pipeline builds the way production builds, then starts the artefact and calls it.
The four tests that exist because of an outage
A child process loads the server with ESM require disabled — the runtime shape that broke in July — and asserts it still
If you remember one line: the pipeline builds the way production builds, then starts the server and calls it. Everything else is a detail around that idea.
No jargon goes unexplained anywhere on this page. This is the whole vocabulary.
The function that answers one URL.
Code that runs before or after every handler.
A method plus a path the server answers.
The wrapper every answer arrives in.
A numbered SQL file that changes the schema.
The table that records which migrations ran.
A rule the database will not break.
A column that must match a row elsewhere.
The column that identifies a row.
A small set of reused connections.
Something the platform calls on a schedule.
Running it twice changes nothing extra.
Started per request, not kept alive.
A library that writes SQL for you.
not used — SQL is written by hand
Which other sites may call the API.
A cap on requests per minute.
Screens compiled into the server build.
The first request after the process stopped.
13 · The gaps — and how to check every claim on this page
Read this before repeating anything above. It is the difference between documentation and advertising.
Anyone with the URL is an admin. The only gate is the hosting provider's
Messages and signatures are recorded, not delivered. No email, no SMS, no e-sign
A daily sweep plus an interval. No queue, no worker, no retry ladder, no
Two append-only logs, but no per-record history and no restore button.
Every write is attributed to usr_owner, so history cannot say who did it.
3,370 lines, 94 handlers. Correct, tested, and the first thing to split.
How to verify this page yourself
Every claim above has a command or a file behind it. In a fresh clone:
npm run verify # all ten gates
npm run test:pg # needs a real PostgreSQL
npm run build:service # then: node apps/api/dist/index.js
Three things could not be observed from outside the deployment, so they are not asserted anywhere on this page.
3 the running function — the URL answers
The build and the deploy steps are verified.
The behaviour after deploy is not.
The test of a good architecture document is not whether it makes the system look impressive. It is whether a reader who trusts it would be surprised later. Nothing on this page should surprise them.
